projects.readme:
# MathBlitz

### Practical math for everyday decisions

MathBlitz turns the numbers behind everyday life into short, interactive challenges: comparing grocery prices, planning savings, understanding interest, measuring a room, checking a utility bill, and making better use of meeting time.

A responsive browser interface and a native Android client share one versioned FastAPI backend. Code-defined scenario templates provide randomized practice across **12 real-world categories** and **five difficulty levels**, with server-checked answers, strategy hints, saved progress, and a leaderboard.

**No Streamlit. No external AI service or API key required. No frontend build step.**

[Quick Start](#quick-start) | [Scenarios](#scenario-library) | [User Journey](#the-end-to-end-flow) | [Architecture](#architecture) | [API](#rest-api) | [Android](#android-app) | [Testing](#testing-and-verification)

![MathBlitz welcome screen with practical math scenarios, five difficulty levels, and account access](docs/images/mathblitz-welcome.jpg)

*Actual application screenshot captured locally on October 28, 2026. Workspace screenshots below use a disposable demo account, not personal user data.*

## The Problem

Everyday decisions often involve useful math hidden inside an ordinary task:

- A larger package is not necessarily the better deal after unused portions are considered.
- Two successive discounts are not the same as adding their percentages.
- A short meeting consumes the combined time of everyone attending.
- A monthly payment difference adds up over years, but is not a complete rent-versus-buy analysis.
- A recipe, room, or electricity bill requires converting units before calculating a result.

MathBlitz focuses on these practical situations rather than disconnected arithmetic worksheets. The aim is to make frequent, approachable number practice useful to people with different interests and confidence levels. It is a practice tool, not a certified cognitive-health intervention or a professional decision engine.

## Who It Is For

| Audience | Useful practice |
| --- | --- |
| Families and younger learners, with adult guidance | Change, sharing, servings, steps, and familiar quantities |
| Students and math-puzzle enthusiasts | Ratios, percentages, estimation, and multi-step reasoning |
| Professionals and office teams | Person-hours, task allocation, commute costs, and budgets |
| Homeowners, renters, and DIY enthusiasts | Space requirements, commissions, property tax, paint, and flooring |
| Educators and math professors | Concrete starting points for explaining assumptions and discussing trade-offs |
| Older adults and casual daily users | Short, repeatable practice with real-life contexts |

The product direction is age-inclusive, but difficulty levels are **not age-calibrated or validated for ages 5-90**. Current tasks are timed and require reading; some contexts remain more suitable for adults. The existing terms specify a minimum self-registration age of 13, and parental-consent controls are not implemented.

## Project Snapshot

| Area | Current implementation |
| --- | --- |
| Browser client | Responsive HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, and inline SVG icons |
| Android client | Native Java client using the same HTTP API |
| Backend | FastAPI, versioned REST endpoints, generated OpenAPI schema |
| Durable storage | SQLAlchemy models; SQLite by default |
| Shared caching | Optional Redis; local in-memory fallback |
| Practice content | 12 category generators, five levels, numeric and two-option answers |
| Feedback | Hints, correct/incorrect/timeout outcomes, points, accuracy, recent attempts |
| Identity | Username/password registration, scrypt hashes, signed expiring bearer tokens |
| Verification | Focused pytest domain, API, security, and legacy-compatibility tests |
| Status | Runnable local application; production hardening and Android device validation remain |

### Practice Workspace

![MathBlitz shopping challenge with level controls, answer input, hint action, and progress cards](docs/images/mathblitz-practice.jpg)

The workspace combines the scenario, level, countdown, answer controls, hints, and recent results. The example above shows an actual buy-two-get-one-free calculation submitted through the API.

### Explore View

![MathBlitz icon-based scenario library covering shopping, finance, housing, office work, and other everyday situations](docs/images/mathblitz-library.jpg)

The library provides a separate exploration view beyond the featured categories. Variation labels in the interface are catalog estimates, as explained below.

## Scenario Library

| Category | Scenario families | Skills | API activity ID |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shopping Value | Unit prices, buy-two-get-one-free offers, package quantities and excess servings | Division, comparison, rounding up | `shopping-value` |
| Discounts & Change | Cash change, successive discounts, sales tax | Addition, subtraction, percentages | `discounts-change` |
| Budget Planner | Daily allowances, savings targets, spending after bills and savings | Division, budgeting, percentages | `budget-planner` |
| Interest & Credit | Simple interest, annual compounding, one-month credit balances | Rates, growth, balance calculations | `interest-credit` |
| Housing Math | Bedroom proportions, split commissions, rent/mortgage differences, property tax | Proportions, percentages, time horizons | `housing-real-estate` |
| Meeting Math | Person-hours, late arrivals, work ratios, shared workloads | Elapsed time, units, allocation | `office-meetings` |
| Commute Costs | Fuel spending, parking/transit comparisons, travel time | Rates, distance, recurring costs | `commute-costs` |
| Build & Measure | Paint coverage, tiles with waste allowance, simplified bracket counts | Area, units, rounding, margins | `build-measure` |
| Health Science | Steps, nutrition-label scaling, sleep duration, rough heart-rate arithmetic | Subtraction, proportions, time | `health-science` |
| Recipe Scaling | Ingredients, cost per serving, whole-pan quantities | Ratios, unit cost, rounding up | `recipe-scaling` |
| Home Utilities | Electricity cost, water use, bill increases | Energy units, rates, percentages | `home-utilities` |
| Quick Estimates | Pizza areas, rough apartment-sampling rules, household water estimates | Geometry, estimation, assumptions | `quick-estimates` |

### Worked Examples

These illustrate supported scenario families; generated numbers vary on each task.

| Situation | Reasoning | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 12 oz costs $3.60; 16 oz costs $4.48 | Compare $3.60 / 12 with $4.48 / 16 | Second package: $0.28/oz versus $0.30/oz |
| A $40 item has 25% off, then another 10% off | $40 x 0.75 x 0.90 | $27.00, not $26.00 from a single 35% discount |
| Keep $10 from a $70 budget lasting seven days | ($70 - $10) / 7 | About $8.57/day |
| Six people attend a 45-minute meeting | 6 x 45 / 60 | 4.5 person-hours |
| A 10 ft by 14 ft room needs 12-inch square tiles and 10% extra | 140 x 1.10; round up | 154 tiles |
| An appliance draws 1,000 W for four hours at $0.20/kWh | (1,000 / 1,000) x 4 x $0.20 | $0.80 |

### Randomized And Choreographed Content

Each generator selects from code-defined scenario families, varies quantities and rates, computes an expected answer, and supplies an approach hint. Difficulty can change number ranges, available branches, or calculation steps.

Here, **choreographed** means deliberately structured templates. It does **not** mean a personalized learning sequence, adaptive curriculum, or AI-generated narrative.

The original content goal is roughly 10,000 variations per category across five levels. The catalog declares estimates of 100,000-130,000 variations per category. These are **metadata estimates, not an enumerated or exhaustively audited puzzle bank**. Tests check generation and declared estimates, not uniqueness of 10,000 prompts per category. Repeated scenarios, equivalent calculations, and ties can occur. Deduplication and a full content-quality audit remain roadmap items.

Generators accept an injected `random.Random` instance for reproducible tests. The public task API does not expose a seed parameter.

## Difficulty And Scoring

| Level | Server time limit | Multiplier | Base points when correct | Intended progression |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Very Easy | 90 seconds | 1x | 10 | Friendly numbers and introductory reasoning |
| Easy | 60 seconds | 2x | 20 | Short calculations with common values |
| Medium | 45 seconds | 3x | 30 | Everyday multi-step reasoning |
| Hard | 30 seconds | 4x | 40 | Larger numbers and less obvious operations |
| Extreme Hard | 20 seconds | 5x | 50 | Faster multi-step calculation |

```text
correct-answer points = (10 x level multiplier)
                      + floor(max(0, time limit - elapsed seconds) / 5)
incorrect or timed-out answer = 0 points
```

The backend owns the deadline and scoring; changing a browser countdown does not extend task expiration. Currency and decimal answers allow an absolute difference of up to `0.01`; integer and choice answers require an exact match. Many non-currency generator outputs are rounded to one decimal place.

Progress includes total attempts, score, accuracy, average response time, a recent correct-answer streak, and correct answers today. The daily goal is 12 correct answers. Daily aggregation uses UTC. The streak counts consecutive correct results within the latest 40 attempts; it is not a consecutive-calendar-day streak.

## The End-to-End Flow

1. **Open the app.** FastAPI serves the browser client and assets; Android connects to the same backend separately.
2. **Register or sign in.** The API validates credentials, hashes new passwords with scrypt, and returns an expiring signed bearer token.
3. **Choose a category and level.** The client loads the public catalog and the user's saved preferences.
4. **Request a scenario.** A generator creates a task; the service stores a user-owned session containing its answer and expiration.
5. **Solve the problem.** The client displays the prompt, answer controls, countdown, and optional hint. The issue response does not include the answer.
6. **Submit once.** The server checks ownership, prior submission, deadline, and answer policy, then records the outcome. A database uniqueness constraint also prevents duplicate attempts.
7. **Receive feedback.** The response includes the correct answer, result status, points, and elapsed duration.
8. **Review progress.** Dashboard and leaderboard queries aggregate durable attempts, using short-lived caches for repeat reads.
9. **Return later.** History and preferences remain in the database. Browser tokens use session storage; Android maintains local client settings.

## Architecture

MathBlitz is a **layered modular monolith**, not a collection of microservices. It separates presentation, HTTP transport, application use cases, domain rules, and persistence while keeping local deployment small.

```text
Responsive web client             Native Android client
          |                                |
          +--------- HTTP /api/v1 ----------+
                           |
               FastAPI routes and validation
                           |
          Authentication / practice / preference services
                     |                 |
              Domain strategies    Repositories and cache port
                                       |           |
                              SQLAlchemy DB     Redis or memory
```

| Boundary | Responsibility | Main location |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Presentation | Screens, icons, form state, countdown rendering, API calls | `frontend/`, `android/` |
| HTTP | Contracts, authentication dependencies, HTTP statuses | `mathblitz/api/`, `mathblitz/schemas.py` |
| Application | Register/login, issue/submit task, progress, preferences | `mathblitz/services.py` |
| Domain | Generator contract, scenarios, levels, answer/scoring policy | `mathblitz/domain/` |
| Persistence | Models, query adapters, sessions, legacy import | `mathblitz/db/` |
| Infrastructure | Settings, security helpers, cache adapters, composition root | `mathblitz/core/` |

### SOLID-Informed Design

- **Single responsibility:** HTTP validation, scoring, generation, and database queries live in distinct modules.
- **Open/closed:** New categories implement `ActivityGenerator` and register an `ActivitySpec` without rewriting task submission.
- **Liskov substitution:** Generators share the `GeneratedTask` contract; memory and Redis adapters share the cache contract.
- **Interface segregation:** Generators and cache consumers use focused interfaces rather than one all-purpose infrastructure object.
- **Dependency inversion:** Domain rules avoid FastAPI/SQLAlchemy dependencies, and caching uses an injected abstract port. Queries are isolated behind concrete repository adapters; repository interfaces are not yet fully abstracted.

Android currently concentrates screens and orchestration in one `MainActivity`. Further modularization is a next step, not a completed clean-architecture claim. See [Architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) for supporting notes.

## Database Design

| Table | Stored data | Important constraints and indexes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `users` | UUID, display/canonical username, password hash, creation time | Unique case-folded username |
| `user_preferences` | Default category, level, sound setting | One row per user; difficulty check |
| `task_sessions` | User, category, level, prompt, hint, answer mode, protected answer, context, timestamps | User foreign key; user/creation-time and expiration indexes |
| `attempts` | Task/user, submitted answer, outcome, points, duration, submission time | Unique task ID; result/level checks; user/time and category/level indexes |

A user has one preference row and many task sessions. A task can have at most one attempt. Separating issued tasks from submitted attempts supports protected answers, server deadlines, and durable results.

SQLite defaults to `data/mathblitz.db`; SQLAlchemy creates missing tables at startup. PostgreSQL-compatible reference DDL is in [`migrations/001_initial.sql`](migrations/001_initial.sql), but there is no automated versioned migration runner. A matching PostgreSQL driver must be installed separately to use a PostgreSQL URL. See [Database Design](docs/DATABASE.md).

## Redis And Scaling

Redis stores ephemeral state, not the source of truth:

- Failed-login counters keyed by client IP and case-folded username.
- Dashboard summaries per user.
- Leaderboard results per requested limit.

Without reachable Redis at startup, the app uses a thread-safe process-local memory adapter. This keeps development self-contained but does not provide shared throttling or coherent caches across workers. A Redis failure after startup has no general runtime failover mechanism.

The intended shared-deployment direction is multiple API workers behind a TLS reverse proxy, PostgreSQL for durable storage, and Redis for shared counters/caches. Static assets can be delivered separately. This structure is **not** a deployed or load-tested cluster included in the repository.

Current operational considerations:

- Only the default top-10 leaderboard cache is explicitly invalidated after submission; other limits can remain stale until their TTL expires.
- No scheduled cleanup worker removes abandoned task sessions.
- Schema changes need a release migration process; `create_all` does not evolve existing tables.
- Backups, metrics, tracing, request-wide rate limits, pool tuning, and capacity testing remain deployment work.

## Technology Stack

| --- | --- |
| API | Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn |
| Persistence | SQLAlchemy 2.x, SQLite; optional PostgreSQL with an added driver |
| Cache | redis-py/Redis, or in-process memory |
| Web | HTML5, CSS Grid/Flexbox, vanilla JavaScript, inline SVG |

projects.readme:
# Book Recommendation System

Discover your next read through an interactive Streamlit app that recommends books with similar reader-rating patterns. Select a familiar title and explore five related books, with titles and cover images.

![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.11%2B-3776AB?logo=python&logoColor=white)
![Streamlit](https://img.shields.io/badge/UI-Streamlit-FF4B4B?logo=streamlit&logoColor=white)
![scikit-learn](https://img.shields.io/badge/ML-scikit--learn-F7931E?logo=scikitlearn&logoColor=white)

## Project preview

![Book Recommendation System running locally](docs/images/book-recommendation-system.png)

*Screenshot of the actual Streamlit application. Cover images come from the dataset's external image URLs; availability depends on the image host.*

## Overview

This project implements item-based collaborative filtering on Book-Crossing reader ratings. Each book is represented by its ratings across readers, and a nearest-neighbor model retrieves books with nearby rating vectors. The application uses a selected book as its starting point; it does not require an account or a personal reading history.

The repository includes the data exploration and training notebook, source datasets, saved model artifacts, and an interactive web application.

## Features

- Search or select a title from the trained catalog of **742 books**.
- Request **five book recommendations** with a single button.
- Browse recommended titles and their cover images in a five-column layout.
- Run inference locally using the included model artifacts.
- Inspect and reproduce data preparation and training in a Jupyter notebook.

## How recommendations work

1. Load book metadata and ratings from the `BX-*.csv` files using Latin-1 encoding and semicolon delimiters.
2. Keep readers with **more than 200 ratings**.
3. Join ratings to book metadata by ISBN.
4. Keep book titles with **at least 50 rating records** in the filtered, joined data.
5. Remove duplicate reader/title pairs and build a book-by-reader matrix, filling missing ratings with zero.
6. Convert the matrix to a SciPy compressed sparse row matrix and fit scikit-learn's `NearestNeighbors(algorithm="brute")`.
7. At inference, request six neighbors and display positions 1–5, assuming the first result is the selected book itself.

The included pivot matrix has **742 rows (books) × 888 columns (readers)**. The model uses scikit-learn's default Minkowski metric with `p=2`, equivalent to Euclidean distance; cosine similarity is not configured.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Book metadata and reader ratings] --> B[Filter and deduplicate]
    B --> C[Book by reader rating matrix]
    C --> D[Nearest-neighbor model]
    E[Selected book] --> D
    D --> F[Five titles and cover images]
```

## Technology

| Component | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Python | Application and training code |
| Streamlit | Interactive book selector and recommendation display |
| pandas and NumPy | Data preparation, tables, and array operations |
| SciPy | Sparse representation of the ratings matrix |
| scikit-learn | Brute-force nearest-neighbor retrieval |
| Jupyter, Matplotlib, Seaborn | Notebook exploration and model development |
| pickle | Serialization of the trained model and supporting data |

## Run locally

Use **Python 3.11** for the best starting point when working with the historical model. The package metadata permits Python 3.11 and newer, but the saved estimator was created with **scikit-learn 1.3.0**. Loading it with another version can produce compatibility warnings or failures; retraining in your chosen environment is recommended for a reproducible deployment.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/vams2krish/ML-Book-Recommendation-System.git
cd ML-Book-Recommendation-System
python -m venv .venv
```

Activate the virtual environment:

```powershell
# Windows PowerShell
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

```bash
# macOS / Linux
source .venv/bin/activate
```

Install dependencies and launch from the repository root:

```bash
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m pip install pandas scipy
python -m streamlit run app.py
```

Open the local URL printed by Streamlit, typically `http://localhost:8501`. Select a book, then click **Show Recommendation**.

`pandas` is explicitly needed to deserialize the saved DataFrames. The existing requirements are unpinned, so they do not recreate the original training environment. For an environment matching the saved estimator, use Python 3.11 and install `scikit-learn==1.3.0` with compatible NumPy, pandas, and SciPy versions, or regenerate all four artifacts together.

## Repository layout

```text
ML-Book-Recommendation-System/
├── app.py                          # Streamlit UI and recommendation functions
├── Book Recommender System.ipynb    # Exploration, preprocessing, training, export
├── artifacts/
│   ├── model.pkl                   # Fitted nearest-neighbor estimator
│   ├── books_name.pkl              # Titles available in the selector
│   ├── book_pivot.pkl              # Book-by-reader rating matrix
│   └── final_rating.pkl            # Filtered metadata, ratings, and image URLs
├── dataset/
│   ├── BX-Books.csv                # Book metadata used by the notebook
│   ├── BX-Book-Ratings.csv          # Ratings used by the notebook
│   ├── BX-Users.csv                # Reader data loaded during exploration
│   ├── books.csv                   # Additional copies in the repository
│   ├── ratings.csv
│   └── users.csv
├── docs/images/                    # Project screenshot
├── src/                            # Local package placeholder
├── requirements.txt                # Runtime dependencies and editable package
├── setup.py                        # Package metadata
├── Procfile                        # Historical Heroku launch command
└── setup.sh                        # Historical Streamlit server configuration
```

## Data and model artifacts

The `BX-*.csv` files contain the Book-Crossing dataset. The notebook uses book titles, authors, publication years, publishers, cover URLs, reader IDs, and ratings. `BX-Users.csv` is explored, but reader demographic fields are not used as model features. The other three CSV files are present but are not referenced by the training notebook.

The dataset and cover images belong to their respective rights holders. Review the original dataset's terms before redistributing or using the data commercially. The project does not establish a separate license for third-party data or artwork.

All four pickle files must remain aligned: the estimator's row indices correspond to `book_pivot.pkl`, while `final_rating.pkl` supplies cover URLs. Only load pickle files from trusted sources, because deserialization can execute code.

## Retrain the model

Install the notebook tools in your activated environment:

```bash
python -m pip install jupyter matplotlib seaborn pandas scipy
python -m jupyter notebook "Book Recommender System.ipynb"
```

Run the notebook cells in order from the repository root. Its export cells overwrite the four files in `artifacts/`. Restart Streamlit after exporting so it loads the regenerated files. The `artifacts/` directory is already included in this repository.

## Deployment

The app can run on a host that supports Python and Streamlit. Install its dependencies, include the trusted artifacts, set the working directory to the repository root, and use:

```bash
python -m streamlit run app.py --server.address 0.0.0.0 --server.port 8501
```

Use the port assigned by your hosting provider when required. `Procfile` and `setup.sh` preserve an older Heroku setup; they are not evidence of a currently available hosted demo.

## Limitations and future improvements

- Recommendations reflect rating patterns, rather than plot, genre, or semantic similarity.
- Only titles in the filtered training catalog are selectable; new books need retraining.
- Missing ratings and any existing zero ratings are both represented as zero in the matrix.
- Grouping by title can combine different editions or books sharing the same title.
- The display skips the first neighbor by position; an explicit selected-title exclusion would handle distance ties more reliably.
- Cover links may be unavailable. The current UI does not provide a fallback image.
- The notebook does not report held-out recommendation metrics, so no accuracy or quality score is claimed.
- Dependency locking, automated evaluation, artifact validation, content-based features, and reader-specific recommendations are possible next steps.

## Author and contributions

Maintained by [Vamshi Krishna](https://github.com/vams2krish). Suggestions and contributions are welcome through GitHub issues and pull requests.

## License

There is currently no standalone `LICENSE` file in this repository. Although the original package metadata mentions MIT, explicit licensing terms should be added before treating the project code as MIT-licensed. Third-party dataset and image rights are separate.

# ML — Boston Housing Price Prediction

![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.11-3776AB?logo=python&logoColor=white) ![Framework](https://img.shields.io/badge/App-Streamlit-FF4B4B?logo=streamlit&logoColor=white) ![Model](https://img.shields.io/badge/Model-Linear_Regression-orange)

An educational machine learning project that estimates historical Boston-area median home values using **multiple linear regression**. It includes an exploratory Jupyter notebook, a Boston Housing CSV dataset, a saved model, and an interactive Streamlit application with 13 feature sliders.

## Project image

![Actual versus predicted home values from the project notebook](docs/images/actual-vs-predicted.png)

*Actual output from the committed notebook: test-set values compared with model predictions. The dashed diagonal represents perfect predictions. Values are in thousands of historical US dollars. This is a model visualization, not a screenshot of the app.*

## What the project does

- Explores dataset dimensions, types, missing values, and descriptive statistics.
- Splits the data into training and test sets with a fixed random seed.
- Fits scikit-learn's `LinearRegression` estimator using all 13 predictors.
- Evaluates predictions with mean squared error and R².
- Visualizes actual versus predicted values and residual errors.
- Loads a serialized estimator in Streamlit and displays an estimate after the user clicks **submit**.

## Dataset and features

`BostonHousing.csv` contains **506 rows**, **13 predictors**, and the target **MEDV**. The notebook's saved inspection reports no missing values.

| Feature | Description |
| --- | --- |
| CRIM | Per-capita crime rate by town |
| ZN | Proportion of residential land zoned for lots over 25,000 square feet |
| INDUS | Proportion of non-retail business acres per town |
| CHAS | Charles River indicator: 1 if the tract borders the river, otherwise 0 |
| NOX | Nitric oxide concentration, in parts per 10 million |
| RM | Average number of rooms per dwelling |
| AGE | Proportion of owner-occupied units built before 1940 |
| DIS | Weighted distance to five Boston employment centers |
| RAD | Index of accessibility to radial highways |
| TAX | Full-value property-tax rate per $10,000 |
| PTRATIO | Pupil–teacher ratio by town |
| B | Historical race-derived variable: 1000 × (Bk − 0.63)²; Bk is the proportion of Black residents by town |
| LSTAT | Percentage classified as lower socioeconomic status in the original dataset terminology |
| MEDV | Target: median value of owner-occupied homes, in $1,000s |

The feature order above matches the app and training notebook. The CSV uses lowercase column names; the app constructs uppercase labels and supplies the same positional order to the estimator.

## Model and recorded results

The notebook uses an **80/20 train/test split**, `random_state=42`, with **404 training rows** and **102 test rows**. It fits ordinary least squares without a scaling pipeline or hyperparameter search.

| Metric | Recorded notebook result |
| --- | ---: |
| Test mean squared error | 24.2911 (thousand dollars)² |
| Test R² | 0.66876 |

These are the notebook's saved results, not a newly executed benchmark or cross-validation estimate. The app multiplies the model output by 1,000 to format a dollar amount. These historical values do not represent current market prices.

## Run locally

Use Python 3.11 or later, starting from the repository root:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/vams2krish/ML-Boston-Housing-Price-Prediction.git
cd ML-Boston-Housing-Price-Prediction
python -m venv .venv
```

Activate the environment:

```powershell
# Windows PowerShell
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

```bash
# macOS / Linux
source .venv/bin/activate
```

Install and launch:

```bash
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m streamlit run app.py
```

Open the local URL printed by Streamlit, adjust the feature sliders, and click **submit** to display the predicted value. Run the command from the repository root so the relative artifact path resolves.

### Explore or retrain in Jupyter

```bash
python -m pip install notebook
python -m notebook
```

Open `House Prediction - Linear Regression.ipynb` and execute cells in order. Its CSV path is relative to the repository root. The notebook writes the fitted estimator to `artifacts/predicted_price.pkl`.

The original final cell also writes the estimator into files named `target_test.pkl`, `target_pred.pkl`, and `residuals.pkl`; those names do **not** indicate saved arrays. Only `predicted_price.pkl` is used by the app.

## Repository structure

```text
.
├── app.py                                  # Streamlit prediction interface
├── BostonHousing.csv                       # Dataset: predictors and MEDV target
├── House Prediction - Linear Regression.ipynb
├── artifacts/
│   └── predicted_price.pkl                  # Serialized fitted estimator
├── docs/images/actual-vs-predicted.png      # Notebook visualization
├── requirements.txt                        # Python dependencies
├── setup.py                                # Local package metadata
├── src/                                    # Local package directory
├── Procfile                                # Legacy Heroku launch command
└── setup.sh                                # Legacy Streamlit deployment setup
```

## Limitations and responsible use

This is a historical learning exercise. The dataset includes a race-derived predictor and socioeconomic terminology that encode problematic assumptions. Retaining these variables documents the original implementation; it does not establish that they are appropriate for real housing decisions.

The model has one fixed test split, no cross-validation, no uncertainty intervals, and no demonstrated performance on current housing data. Linear regression can produce unrealistic values for unusual inputs, and some slider bounds extend beyond the observed training range. Use it for studying regression and app integration, not property appraisal, lending, or other consequential decisions.

Dependencies are currently unpinned. Pickled scikit-learn models can be incompatible across versions; if loading fails, retrain with the installed environment. Only load pickle files from a trusted source.

## Technology

Python · pandas · NumPy · scikit-learn · Matplotlib · Jupyter Notebook · Streamlit

## Author and licensing

**Vamshi Krishna Adam** — [GitHub](https://github.com/vams2krish)

The package metadata declares MIT, but this repository does not currently include a standalone LICENSE file. Dataset redistribution terms should be checked separately before reuse.

# ML - Customer Segmentation Mall

**Unsupervised machine learning (ML) for exploring customer groups with K-Means clustering.**

This project explores mall customer demographics, annual income, and spending behavior through a Python notebook. It demonstrates data inspection, feature preparation, standardization, cluster exploration, model fitting, visualization, and assigning a sample customer to a segment. Customer groups can provide a starting point for targeted marketing hypotheses and customer engagement planning.

![Project elbow-method visualization](docs/images/elbow-method.png)

*Project image extracted from the notebook's saved output: within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS) across candidate cluster counts.*

## ML or DL?

This is a **machine learning (ML)** project, specifically **unsupervised learning / clustering**. It uses scikit-learn's K-Means to group records without labeled target outcomes. It is **not deep learning (DL)**: no neural networks or deep learning frameworks are used.

## Dataset

`archive/Mall_Customers.csv` contains **200 records and five columns**:

| Column | Description | Current model usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CustomerID` | Customer identifier | Included as a numeric feature |
| `Genre` | Categorical gender field, using the CSV's original name | Encoding demonstrated separately; excluded from clustering |
| `Age` | Customer age | Included |
| `Annual Income (k$)` | Annual income in thousands of dollars | Included |
| `Spending Score (1-100)` | Dataset spending score | Included |

The notebook checks dataset shape, missing values, and categories. The original dataset source and redistribution license are not recorded in the supplied files; no specific provenance or license is asserted here.

## Methodology

1. Load the CSV with pandas and inspect the data.
2. Drop `Genre` to create a numeric feature matrix.
3. Standardize the numeric features using `StandardScaler`.
4. Demonstrate one-hot encoding of `Genre` separately.
5. Fit K-Means for 1–10 clusters and plot inertia using the elbow method.
6. Fit a five-cluster model with `init='k-means++'` and `random_state=42`.
7. Append cluster labels to the dataframe in memory and visualize segments.
8. Scale a sample customer record and predict its cluster assignment.

Cluster identifiers are arbitrary labels, not customer rankings or validated business categories.

## Technology

- Python and Jupyter Notebook
- pandas and NumPy for data handling
- scikit-learn for preprocessing and clustering
- Matplotlib for visualization
- Seaborn, imported in the notebook

## Run locally

```bash
git clone https://github.com/vams2krish/ML-Customer-Segmentation-Mall.git
cd ML-Customer-Segmentation-Mall
python -m venv .venv
```

Activate the environment in Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

Or on macOS / Linux:

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
```

Install dependencies and launch the notebook:

```bash
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
jupyter notebook Customer-Segmentation-Mall.ipynb
```

Before running the cells, replace the original machine-specific CSV path with:

```python
customer_dataset = pd.read_csv("archive/Mall_Customers.csv")
```

Run from the repository root using a Python version supported by the scientific packages. Dependencies are unpinned and do not represent a verified runtime environment. The notebook's `sparse_output` argument requires scikit-learn 1.2 or newer.

## Outputs

- Elbow-method chart comparing candidate cluster counts.
- Five cluster labels added to the in-memory customer dataframe.
- A saved customer-segment scatter plot.
- A sample prediction; the stored output reports cluster `3`.

Saved outputs are from an earlier notebook run and have not been regenerated for publication. Five clusters are selected in the code; no silhouette score, stability analysis, or external validation is reported. Assignments can vary with library versions and initialization defaults.

## Known limitations

- **Feature selection:** `CustomerID` participates in clustering. Remove this identifier before drawing business conclusions, since identifiers generally should not determine customer similarity.
- **Plot labels:** the segment scatter plot uses standardized `CustomerID` and `Age` (columns 0 and 1), although its labels say income and spending score. Correct the selected columns or labels before interpreting it.
- **Centroids:** the segment plot references lowercase `kmeans` from the elbow loop rather than the five-cluster `Kmeans` model. Use the five-cluster model's centroids for a consistent plot.
- **Encoding:** the one-hot encoded category values are not combined with the model features.
- **Reproducibility:** explicitly set `n_init` and pin a tested environment to avoid changes in library defaults.
- **Validation:** compare cluster quality, stability, and segment profiles before applying results to business decisions.
- **Scope:** this is an exploratory notebook with a small dataset, not a deployed service or a validated production segmentation system. No trained model export is included.

## Repository structure

```text
ML-Customer-Segmentation-Mall/
├── Customer-Segmentation-Mall.ipynb   # Original exploratory notebook
├── archive/
│   └── Mall_Customers.csv            # Input data
├── docs/images/
│   └── elbow-method.png              # Saved notebook chart
```

projects.readme:
# ML - Zoo Animal Classification

![Wildlife cover featuring a variety of animals](docs/images/zoo-cover.png)

*AI-generated wildlife cover artwork; illustrative, not an application screenshot.*

An educational machine learning project that explores animal traits, trains a **K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)** classifier, and provides a **Streamlit interface** for predicting an animal name from 16 biological attributes.

The repository brings together a dataset, an exploratory Jupyter notebook, a serialized model, and an interactive prediction app. It is a learning prototype: the saved evaluation shows **0% test accuracy**, and the preprocessing needs correction before predictions can be considered reliable.

## Project overview

- Explore animal records with descriptive statistics, missing-value checks, and visualizations.
- Examine feature relationships with a correlation heatmap.
- Train a five-neighbor classifier with scikit-learn.
- Inspect a confusion matrix and classification report.
- Enter traits using sliders and display a predicted animal name in Streamlit.

Despite the app title referring to animal “type,” the notebook's target is `animal_name`, not broad categories such as mammal, bird, or reptile. The model uses structured traits rather than photographs; this is not an image-recognition system.

## Dataset and features

The included file, [`archive/zoo_data-1.csv`](archive/zoo_data-1.csv), contains **101 records**, **100 distinct animal names**, and **17 columns**: the target plus 16 input features. The repository does not currently document the dataset's original source or redistribution license.

| Feature | Meaning | Input |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hair` | Has hair | 0 / 1 |
| `feathers` | Has feathers | 0 / 1 |
| `eggs` | Lays eggs | 0 / 1 |
| `milk` | Produces milk | 0 / 1 |
| `airborne` | Can fly | 0 / 1 |
| `aquatic` | Aquatic animal | 0 / 1 |
| `predator` | Predatory animal | 0 / 1 |
| `toothed` | Has teeth | 0 / 1 |
| `backbone` | Has a backbone | 0 / 1 |
| `breathes` | Breathes air | 0 / 1 |
| `venomous` | Venomous | 0 / 1 |
| `fins` | Has fins | 0 / 1 |
| `legs` | Number of legs | App accepts integers from 0 to 8 |
| `tail` | Has a tail | 0 / 1 |
| `domestic` | Domestic animal | 0 / 1 |
| `catsize` | Cat-sized or larger indicator | 0 / 1 |

For binary features, `0` means no and `1` means yes. The feature descriptions reflect the column conventions; an authoritative dataset dictionary is not included.

## Repository structure

```text
ML-Zoo-Animal-Classification/
|-- README.md                              # Project documentation
|-- app.py                                 # Streamlit prediction interface
|-- Zoo-Animal-Classification-ML.ipynb       # Exploration, training, evaluation
|-- model.pkl                              # Serialized KNN estimator
|-- requirements.txt                       # Existing core dependencies
|-- archive/
|   `-- zoo_data-1.csv                      # Animal traits and names
`-- docs/images/
    `-- zoo-cover.png                      # Illustrative wildlife cover
```

## Run the application locally

Install Python with `venv` support, then clone the repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/vams2krish/ML-Zoo-Animal-Classification.git
cd ML-Zoo-Animal-Classification
python -m venv .venv
```

Activate the environment:

```powershell
# Windows PowerShell
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

```bash
# macOS / Linux
source .venv/bin/activate
```

Install the packages used by the app and notebook:

```bash
python -m pip install streamlit pandas numpy matplotlib seaborn scikit-learn jupyter
python -m streamlit run app.py
```

Run the command from the repository root so the app can find `model.pkl`. Open the local URL printed by Streamlit, set the trait sliders, and click **submit** to display a predicted animal name. The current implementation calculates a prediction on each Streamlit rerun; the button controls when it is displayed.

The existing `requirements.txt` lists unpinned core dependencies and omits Streamlit, Seaborn, and Jupyter; the install command above includes these. There is no tested Python-version matrix. The notebook metadata records Python 3.11.5, but the environment used to export the model is not fully documented. Serialized estimators can be version-sensitive. Only load pickle files from sources you trust.

## Explore and train in the notebook

```bash
python -m jupyter notebook Zoo-Animal-Classification-ML.ipynb
```

Before running the notebook, replace the machine-specific `filePath` assignment in the data-loading cell with:

```python
filePath = "archive/zoo_data-1.csv"
```

The notebook currently follows these steps:

1. Load the CSV and inspect its contents, summary statistics, and missing values.
2. Plot animal-name counts and feature correlations.
3. Separate `animal_name` from the 16 input features.
4. Split records into 80% training and 20% test data with `random_state=42`.
5. Apply `StandardScaler` and fit `KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)`.
6. Generate predictions, a confusion matrix, and a classification report.
7. Predict an example record and save the estimator as `model.pkl`.

Running the export cell overwrites `model.pkl` in the working directory.

## Evaluation and current limitations

The **stored notebook output** reports accuracy of **0.00 on 21 test records**. This is an existing recorded result, not a newly reproduced benchmark. No claim of production readiness or accurate animal identification is made.

Several implementation choices explain why further work is needed:

- **Sparse target labels:** 100 distinct names across 101 rows leave almost no repeated examples per class. Many test labels have no training examples, so a classifier cannot learn to recognize those names from this split.
- **Test preprocessing:** the notebook calls `fit_transform` separately on the training and test sets. It should fit the scaler on training data and use `transform` for test data. The current test transformation also replaces the scaler's fitted state before the example prediction.
- **Training/inference mismatch:** the model is trained on scaled features, but the Streamlit app passes raw slider values. Only the KNN estimator is saved; the scaler is not exported with it.
- **Portability:** the notebook uses a machine-specific absolute dataset path, and dependencies are not pinned.
- **Input validation:** sliders allow biologically inconsistent combinations and leg counts that may be outside the dataset's observed examples.

## Suggested next steps

1. Choose a target supported by enough repeated examples; if broad animal groups are desired, add a verified class label and document its source.
2. Use a scikit-learn `Pipeline` containing `StandardScaler` and KNN, and save the entire pipeline for consistent inference.
3. Evaluate with an appropriate split or cross-validation strategy after resolving the target-label problem.
4. Pin and test dependencies, make the dataset path portable, and add clear app error handling.
5. Document dataset provenance and licensing, then add validated example predictions and an actual interface screenshot.

## Technology

**Python · pandas · NumPy · scikit-learn · Matplotlib · Seaborn · Jupyter · Streamlit · pickle**

## Author and licensing

Maintained by [Vamshi Krishna Adam](https://github.com/vams2krish).

No software license is currently included in this repository. Public visibility alone does not grant an open-source license. Dataset licensing must also be confirmed separately.

# PortfolioBot ☺ **Vamshi Krishna Adam’s personal portfolio, with an AI sidekick that has done the reading.** A minimal, playful portfolio that combines an illustrated project gallery, a local retrieval-augmented AI chat, and a direct path to a real conversation. Visitors can explore public GitHub projects, ask questions grounded in project documentation, or book a 30-minute discovery call. ![PortfolioBot desktop preview: a playful personal portfolio with a smiling AI sidekick](docs/assets/portfolio-hero.png) [Meet the builder](https://linkedin.com/in/adamvamshikrishna) · [Explore the code](https://github.com/vams2krish) · [Book a 30-minute hello](https://calendly.com/adam-vamshikrishna/vamshi-intro-meeting-30-mins-chat) ## What it does - **Personal introduction:** a human-first hero, about section, skills, contact details, and a smiling digital sidekick. - **GitHub project gallery:** all public repositories imported from `vams2krish`, with searchable descriptions, category filters, illustrated covers, detail dialogs, and repository links. - **Automatic updates:** the running server refreshes GitHub every five minutes, open browsers update their gallery every minute, and GitHub Actions refreshes the committed snapshot every 30 minutes. - **Grounded AI chat:** a local Ollama model answers using retrieved profile information and public GitHub README excerpts. Responses include source labels and repository links. - **Discovery-call booking:** meeting and booking questions return a validated Calendly button immediately, without waiting for model inference. - **Optional local image generation:** AUTOMATIC1111 can generate an abstract avatar through its Stable Diffusion API. The CSS mascot works without it. - **Honest fallback:** if Ollama is unavailable or times out, the chat shows clearly identified source excerpts instead of presenting them as AI-generated answers. - **A little goofiness:** fictional desk-object reviews have varied star ratings and explicit demo labels. They are excluded from factual retrieval. - **Responsive layout:** desktop and mobile designs, keyboard-accessible controls, reduced-motion support, and native project dialogs. ## Project photos These are screenshots of the running application. Individual gallery covers are original illustrations, not screenshots of those separate projects.
Full desktop page ![Full desktop portfolio, including projects, about, demo reviews, and contact](docs/assets/portfolio-desktop.png)
Mobile page
## Quick start **Requirements:** Node.js 20+ and, for generated chat answers, a running local Ollama installation with a chat model. There are no npm runtime dependencies and no build step. ```bash git clone https://github.com/vams2krish/PortfolioBot.git cd PortfolioBot npm start ``` Open **http://127.0.0.1:4175**. Browsing projects, viewing contact details, and booking a call work without Ollama. To prepare the preferred chat model in a separate terminal: ```bash ollama pull llama3.2 ollama serve ``` If the Ollama desktop app is already serving, another `ollama serve` process is unnecessary. ## Configuration Set environment variables in the shell before starting the server: | Variable | Default | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | `PORT` | `4175` | Local web-server port | | `OLLAMA_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:11434` | Ollama API base URL | | `OLLAMA_MODEL` | Automatic local selection | Override the chat model | | `AUTOMATIC1111_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:7860` | AUTOMATIC1111 API base URL | | `GITHUB_AUTO_SYNC` | `true` | Set to `false` to disable the running server's GitHub refresh | | `GITHUB_SYNC_INTERVAL_SECONDS` | `300` | Runtime refresh interval, with a minimum of 60 seconds | PowerShell example: ```powershell $env:PORT = '4175' $env:OLLAMA_URL = 'http://127.0.0.1:11434' $env:OLLAMA_MODEL = 'llama3.2:latest' $env:AUTOMATIC1111_URL = 'http://127.0.0.1:7860' npm start ``` Automatic selection prefers installed `llama3.2:latest`, then `qwen2.5:7b`, then another eligible local model. Cloud-backed, embedding, OCR, and vision-named models are excluded from automatic selection. Choose a model your hardware can load. `.env.example` documents the settings. The application **does not automatically load `.env` files**; export settings in your shell. No OpenAI key or paid API is needed. ## How the retrieval chat works ```text Visitor question │ ├─ Booking/contact request ──► profile details + Calendly button │ ▼ Profile + GitHub metadata + README chunks │ ▼ Keyword relevance scoring → top 5 source passages │ ▼ Local Ollama chat model → answer + source links │ └─ Inference fails → explicitly labeled direct excerpts ``` `retrieval.mjs` turns the profile, project summaries, and README chunks into searchable documents. It removes common stop words, scores matching words and source titles, and selects five passages for the model context. README chunks are approximately 1,400 characters. This is **lightweight lexical RAG**: it does not use embeddings, a vector database, or semantic reranking. It is easy to inspect and runs without an indexing service. The prompt tells the model to use only the supplied context, avoid inventing facts, and treat retrieved text as data rather than instructions. These instructions reduce unsupported answers but do not guarantee accuracy. Questions are standalone; conversation history is not currently sent to the model. Source labels show the retrieved passages, rather than a verified citation for every generated claim. ## GitHub import The portfolio automatically discovers **all currently public repositories** from `vams2krish`. The gallery shows the latest repository total and refresh status. The table below highlights the original project collection; the live gallery includes subsequent additions too. | Project | Focus | | --- | --- | | [ResearchPal](https://github.com/vams2krish/ResearchPal) | Local research-paper reading, AI explanations, synthesis, and flashcards | | [MathBlitz](https://github.com/vams2krish/MathBlitz) | Practical math exercises with a FastAPI backend | | [ClariSEE](https://github.com/vams2krish/ClariSEE) | Text-to-diagram, quiz, and summary experiences in Flutter | | [PDRides](https://github.com/vams2krish/PDRides) | Community carpooling with messaging bots | | [OCR](https://github.com/vams2krish/OCR) | Text extraction from images and PDF documents | | [Books Recommendation System](https://github.com/vams2krish/Books-Recommendation-system) | Collaborative filtering and nearest-neighbor recommendations | | [Zoo Animal Classification](https://github.com/vams2krish/Zoo-Animal-Classification-ML) | Animal-feature classification and exploratory analysis | | [Kidney Prediction](https://github.com/vams2krish/Kidney-prediction-deep-learning) | Deep-learning image-classification project | | [Image Classification](https://github.com/vams2krish/Image-Classification) | Neural networks and TensorFlow data pipelines | | [Boston Housing Regression](https://github.com/vams2krish/Boston-Housing-Price-Linear-Regression) | Linear-regression learning project and interactive predictions | | [simple-browser](https://github.com/vams2krish/simple-browser) | Public repository without a published description or README at initial import | Updates happen automatically: - **While the app runs:** it checks GitHub on startup and every five minutes. Newly public repositories, descriptions, languages, topics, stars, archived/fork status, push timestamps, and README changes flow into both the gallery and the AI context. Private repositories are excluded, and deleted or newly private repositories disappear after a successful refresh. - **While the app is off:** `.github/workflows/sync-portfolio.yml` checks every 30 minutes and commits changed snapshots and cover art to `main`. GitHub may delay scheduled workflows. This keeps the repository ready for the next clone or deployment; it does not start your local server or pull commits into an existing checkout. - **In an open browser:** the gallery checks the server every minute and when the tab becomes visible. Active filters and searches are preserved. Changes usually appear within about six minutes while the app is running, plus network/import time. This uses polling rather than instant GitHub webhooks. The knowledge base includes repository metadata and README text, not an index of every source file. To refresh immediately: ```bash npm run sync:github ``` The shared sync service follows every public-repository page, fetches available README files, and regenerates local SVG cover art. Public GitHub API rate limits apply; no personal token is required. Data is saved in the single `data/github-snapshot.json` file. New covers are prepared first, then the snapshot is replaced atomically so requests see a complete version. On GitHub failure, timeout, or rate limiting, the last successful snapshot remains available. Refreshes are deduplicated within the server, and retries respect GitHub's rate-limit reset time. README imports are capped at 16,000 characters per repository. The workflow commits only when imported content changes. PortfolioBot's own push timestamp is excluded to prevent a loop of commits caused by the sync bot itself. The workflow uses the repository's built-in Actions token for commits; it does not store a personal GitHub credential. Check its run history under the repository's **Actions** tab, or run it manually with **Run workflow**. ## Make it your own Edit `profile.json` to update: - Name, role, location, biography, experience, and skills. - Email, phone number, LinkedIn, GitHub, and HTTPS Calendly link. - Additional manually curated projects and reviews. The server reads profile and snapshot data on each request. The gallery updates automatically after successful syncs; reload for manual biography or contact edits. Edit `github.mjs` for categories, ordering, and fallback descriptions. Current GitHub descriptions take precedence over curated fallback descriptions. Update `public/style.css` and `public/playful.css` for layout and visual styling. Restart the server after changing the GitHub username or environment settings. For a real approved testimonial, use: ```json { "quote": "An approved quote from a real collaborator.", "name": "Collaborator name", "role": "Their role or relationship", "rating": 5, "demo": false } ``` The current homepage review heading and disclosure deliberately describe fictional demo reviews. Update that page copy as well when replacing the section with genuine testimonials. ## Optional AUTOMATIC1111 avatar Start AUTOMATIC1111 with API access enabled (`--api`) and a checkpoint selected, then run: ```powershell Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post http://127.0.0.1:4175/api/avatar ``` The endpoint requests a 512×512 abstract image, saves it to `public/generated/avatar.png`, and returns its local URL. Refresh the portfolio to display it. Generated images are ignored by Git. This creates abstract avatar artwork, not a portrait of Vamshi. The included screenshots show the CSS sidekick. The AUTOMATIC1111 integration is implemented, but live generation has not been verified because the service was offline during development. ## API reference | Method | Endpoint | Behavior | | --- | --- | --- | | `GET` | `/api/profile` | Public profile and merged project metadata; omits README bodies | | `GET` | `/api/status` | Ollama and AUTOMATIC1111 availability and installed Ollama model names | | `POST` | `/api/chat` | Accepts `{"message":"What is ResearchPal?"}`; returns a grounded answer or explicit excerpt fallback | | `POST` | `/api/avatar` | Requests local image generation and saves the returned avatar | Chat questions are limited to 2,000 characters. Ollama inference has a 120-second timeout, and avatar generation has a 180-second timeout. The contact and booking path skips inference. ## Project structure ```text PortfolioBot/ ├── server.mjs # Local HTTP server and model integrations ├── retrieval.mjs # Source documents, chunking, ranking, booking validation ├── github.mjs # GitHub snapshot loading and gallery summaries ├── github-sync.mjs # Automatic refresh, safe snapshot replacement, retries ├── profile.json # Personal details and editable content ├── data/ │ └── github-snapshot.json # Public metadata and README text in one snapshot ├── public/ │ ├── index.html # Portfolio and chat interface │ ├── app.js # Gallery, filters, dialogs, and chat interactions │ ├── style.css # Base layout and responsive styles │ ├── playful.css # Playful visual treatment and CSS mascot │ └── assets/projects/ # Generated SVG project-cover illustrations ├── scripts/ │ ├── sync-github.mjs # Paginated public repository and README import │ └── create-covers.mjs # Local cover-art generation ├── test/ # Retrieval, snapshot, and booking tests └── docs/assets/ # Actual desktop and mobile screenshots ``` ## Validation ```bash npm test ``` Automated tests cover source ranking, README retrieval and links, complete project-list retrieval, exclusion of fictional reviews, booking intent, Calendly URL validation, cover/knowledge coverage, paginated discovery, changed/new/removed/private repositories, unchanged snapshots, failed imports, overlapping refreshes, and rate-limit backoff. Development checks also verified a live Ollama response about ResearchPal, the booking response, and page/asset requests. Browser checks verified all 11 gallery cards, the AI-tools category filter, and no horizontal overflow at a 390px mobile viewport. Screenshots above come from the running local app. ## Local development and deployment boundaries The server binds to `127.0.0.1` and is intended for local development. Publishing this repository does **not** deploy a working public website. A hosted app cannot reach Ollama or AUTOMATIC1111 on a visitor’s or developer’s loopback address. Before public hosting, provide a securely reachable model backend, configure the deployment’s network access, and add request throttling and access controls for expensive model/image operations. The application currently has no authentication or rate limiting. Google Fonts are loaded remotely; replace them with local fonts if you require a fully offline UI. Keep credentials out of source control. `.env` files, generated avatar files, logs, and dependencies are ignored. Public profile information and imported public README text are intentionally part of this repository. ## Contact **Vamshi Krishna Adam** · USA - [Email](mailto:adam.vamshikrishnaz@gmail.com) - [LinkedIn](https://linkedin.com/in/adamvamshikrishna) - [GitHub](https://github.com/vams2krish) - [Book a discovery call](https://calendly.com/adam-vamshikrishna/vamshi-intro-meeting-30-mins-chat) Built with code, curiosity, and a suspicious number of tabs.

projects.readme: # ResearchPal **Read the whole document. Understand the evidence. Turn what you learn into an explanation.** ResearchPal is a local-first reading and research workspace for desktop and mobile browsers. Import PDF, DOCX, Markdown or text; read its complete extracted source; listen to narration; generate study material; and create an editable, narrated video explainer. Version **0.2.0** adds task-specific model connections, automatic Ollama storage discovery, a full Markdown reader, source audio exports, Explainer Studio and a redesigned responsive interface. Electron wraps the same workspace as a desktop app. ![ResearchPal full document reader and narration controls](docs/images/researchpal-reader.png) *Actual interface screenshots use synthetic demonstration material. Automated screenshots use a test text service; narration and MP4 assembly use real Windows speech and FFmpeg.* [Problem](#the-problem) · [Features](#features) · [Setup](#quick-start) · [Models](#models-and-connections) · [Architecture](#architecture) · [Verification](#verification) · [Limitations](#limitations) ## The problem Understanding a research paper means connecting its problem, methods, assumptions, equations, evaluation conditions and limitations. Reading several papers adds the challenge of remembering which source supports which claim. Conventional workflows scatter this work between PDF readers, notes, chat, citations and flashcards. Short summaries can drop the conditions and qualifications that give a finding meaning. ResearchPal combines these activities while retaining the complete extracted source. Reading does not require generating a summary first. The application serves students learning technical literature, researchers organizing evidence, engineers comparing methods, and independent learners building a review routine. Generated output is an aid to investigation, not independent scientific verification. ## The end-to-end workflow 1. **Connect:** discover local/cloud models in Settings and choose a provider/model for each task. 2. **Import:** add a document. Import does not automatically start text-generation or embedding jobs; configured OCR can run during PDF extraction. 3. **Read:** explore full Markdown, follow its outline, inspect raw source or download the `.md` file. 4. **Listen:** use a device voice, or explicitly generate exported narration of every extracted source part. 5. **Study:** generate anatomy, explanations, formulas, claims, glossary terms and flashcards; check them against the source. 6. **Question:** ask about one paper, compare papers, synthesize evidence or investigate with web research. 7. **Explain:** generate or write a storyboard, edit every scene, then choose local slides, generated images or generated motion. 8. **Reuse:** download narrated MP4, complete MP3, source Markdown, notes, citations or Anki TSV, and return for spaced review. ## Features | Area | What is available | | --- | --- | | Library | PDF/DOCX/Markdown/text, favorites, tags, collections and immediate source reading. | | Markdown reader | Full extracted document, outline, tables, lists, code, math, raw source and download; sanitized HTML. | | Full narration | Device voices with pause/resume, speed and part controls; exported MP3 parts, playlist and combined full-document MP3. | | Paper anatomy | Title/Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Experimental Setup, Results, Related Work, Discussion, Conclusion, References, Appendix. | | Section analysis | Long sections are visited in bounded parts rather than silently clipping tails; original headings are retained. | | Evidence | Formulas, figures/tables/code, claim/evidence/assumption/limitation cards and generated first-principles breakdowns. | | Learning | Mind maps, diagrams, glossary, mental models, section notes, human-written notes and FSRS flashcards. | | Original PDF | PDF.js reading, highlights and image-region questions through the selected vision model. | | Research | Retrieved paper questions, synthesis/critique, 2–4-paper comparison, bounded web search/fetch research. | | Explainer Studio | Document/text → editable storyboard → narrated H.264/AAC MP4 with slides, images or motion. | | Connections | Separate text, vision, embedding, image, video, speech and OCR routes; discovery or manual IDs/URLs. | | Local storage | Structural Ollama folder discovery, manual override and optional desktop-managed Ollama startup. | | Jobs | Persisted progress/results for narration, storyboards, video and reindexing; visible interruption without paid resubmission. | | Interface | Light/dark themes, focused navigation, responsive reading and mobile bottom navigation. | | Exports | Source Markdown, study notes, BibTeX, Anki TSV, audio and video. | ### Library and Studio ![ResearchPal library](docs/images/researchpal-library.png) ![Editable storyboard and completed narrated video](docs/images/researchpal-studio.png) ### Mobile reading The responsive browser/PWA interface is the tested mobile path. Separate SwiftUI source under `ios-native/` remains experimental and uncompiled, without browser feature parity. ## Quick start ### Requirements Python 3.11, Git and a modern browser are the documented development baseline. Local generation/embeddings require Ollama with models installed; cloud features need the selected provider's credentials. Node.js/npm is needed only for Electron development/packaging. Hardware requirements depend on the models; no benchmarked minimum is published. ### Windows PowerShell ```powershell git clone https://github.com/vams2krish/ResearchPal.git cd ResearchPal py -3.11 -m venv .venv .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements.txt Copy-Item .env.example .env .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m uvicorn server:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8501 ``` ### macOS / Linux ```bash git clone https://github.com/vams2krish/ResearchPal.git cd ResearchPal python3.11 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt cp .env.example .env .venv/bin/python -m uvicorn server:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8501 ``` Open [the local app](http://127.0.0.1:8501) and configure Settings. [Interactive API docs](http://127.0.0.1:8501/docs) come from FastAPI. The frontend has no separate build/dev server. Reading text documents needs no model; analysis, indexing and media require their task routes. ### Desktop and installer After Python setup: ```bash cd desktop npm install npm start ``` The shell chooses an available loopback port and verifies its backend's instance identity. It does not assume a fixed-port server belongs to this app. Build the Windows installer from the repository root: ```powershell .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install pyinstaller cd desktop npm install npm run dist ``` Output: `desktop/dist/ResearchPal Setup 0.2.0.exe`. PyInstaller bundles Python and FFmpeg; electron-builder creates the installer. Model weights and OCR inference runtimes are not bundled. Application data stays outside the executable. Choosing a different existing library folder in desktop Settings requires restart and does not copy the old library automatically. macOS scripts exist, but macOS packaging/native iOS compilation are not verified by this Windows workflow. ## Models and connections ![Task-specific model configuration](docs/images/researchpal-settings.png) Settings distinguishes a **service connection** from the **model used for a task**. A folder path is not a service URL; model storage belongs to the serving application. | Connection | Tasks | Configuration | | --- | --- | --- | | Ollama | Text, vision, embeddings | Service URL, model IDs, optional storage folder for app-managed startup. | | Gemini | Text, vision | Key and available model ID. | | OpenRouter | Text, vision, embeddings, images, video, speech | Key, base URL, capability-appropriate model IDs; dedicated image/video discovery. | | Compatible API | Text, vision, embeddings, images, video, speech | User URL/key; server must implement each selected protocol. | | ComfyUI | Images, video | Service, API-format workflow, positive prompt node/input, optional checkpoint. | | Automatic1111 | Images | WebUI with `--api`, service URL, checkpoint. | | Unlimited-OCR 2 | OCR | Separate upstream SGLang server, `/v1` URL and served model ID. | | Baidu cloud OCR | OCR | API/secret keys and OCR service access; separate from Unlimited-OCR. | | Device speech | Immediate reading | Device/browser voice; no server audio export. | | Windows speech | Offline audio/video export | Installed voice; blank model field selects its default. | | Edge speech | Online audio/video export | Neural voice ID or default. | Nano Banana and Seedance are model families, not universal API identifiers. Discover or enter the exact models offered by the provider/account; not every model supports every modality. ### Moving Ollama models 1. Open **Settings → Ollama → Find model folders automatically**. 2. Optionally enter a search folder/drive. Discovery checks for `manifests`/`blobs`, skips dependency/system directories and reports search limits. 3. Select a location or enter a manual path, then Save. 4. If no service runs, desktop can start Ollama with this folder. Otherwise restart the external service with updated `OLLAMA_MODELS`; ResearchPal does not take it over. 5. Discover service model IDs and assign task models. No machine-specific model directory is committed in source. Windows discovery reads current user environment settings rather than only an inherited desktop environment. ComfyUI/Automatic1111 checkpoint folders remain server-owned. ### Cloud use and costs Studio displays selected task providers/models before Generate. Image/video modes request one visual generation per scene; long narration needs multiple speech calls. Jobs start only on explicit actions. The UI disables silent cross-provider fallback; restart does not resubmit paid jobs automatically. Provider pricing, quota, access and parameters are external constraints. Discovery does not prove generation access for every listed model. See [the integration guide](docs/providers.md) for endpoint contracts and upstream references. ## Reading, narration and OCR Source narration uses extracted words, removes visual markup/file paths, visits all bounded parts and creates MP3 parts, a playlist and a combined MP3. The older PDF narration action is labelled **study summary** to distinguish it from full source narration. Spoken interpretation of mathematics, tables and layout depends on extraction and voice quality. Automatic OCR detects image pages with little readable text. Always OCR parses the full PDF; Off accepts partial native extraction. Unlimited-OCR sends ordered page images to SGLang and checks page markers/output-budget completion. Baidu cloud OCR handles pages individually and reports quota/service errors. There is no fixed application page-count cutoff. Memory, payload size, token budgets and inference time still bound practical workloads. Unlimited-OCR is a separate GPU service; its upstream example uses an A800 with 80 GB memory. Installing ResearchPal does not install those weights or make a small GPU sufficient. See [upstream setup](https://github.com/baidu/Unlimited-OCR). DOCX retains text and recognized headings, not complete Word layout, embedded media or rich table structure. Convert `.doc` to `.docx` first. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD A[PDF / DOCX / Markdown / text] --> B[Extract source; optional OCR] B --> C[SQLite library and full reader] C --> D[Device speech / full-source audio export] C --> E[Explicit study generation and retrieval] C --> F[Editable Studio storyboard] F --> G[Local slides / provider images / provider video] G --> H[Speech and local FFmpeg assembly] H --> I[Downloadable narrated MP4] J[Connections and capability routes] --> D J --> E J --> F ``` | Layer | Implementation | | --- | --- | | Interface | HTML/CSS/JS modules, Marked/DOMPurify, responsive desktop/mobile views. | | API | FastAPI/Uvicorn, source imports, connections, jobs/progress. | | Data | SQLite, documents, connection settings, job manifests and local media. | | Models | Ollama/Gemini/OpenRouter/compatible APIs, separate capability routes. | | Retrieval | Configurable embeddings in SQLite BLOBs; NumPy cosine ranking. | | Parsing | PyMuPDF4LLM/PyMuPDF, DOCX XML extraction, optional OCR servers. | | Media | Device speech, Windows SAPI, Edge/cloud speech, Pillow, FFmpeg H.264/AAC. | | Learning | FSRS, KaTeX, PDF.js, Mermaid, Markmap/D3; DDGS/Requests/BeautifulSoup research. | | Distribution | Electron, PyInstaller, Windows NSIS installer. | ### Repository map ```text ResearchPal/ ├── server.py # API and analysis queue ├── core/ │ ├── providers.py # Connections, discovery and task routing │ ├── model_storage.py # Ollama folder discovery │ ├── documents.py # Extraction and OCR │ ├── jobs.py # Persisted jobs and bounded workers │ ├── media.py # Narration, storyboards, image/video adapters │ ├── pipeline.py # Anatomy and research analysis │ ├── vectorstore.py # Source chunks and semantic search │ └── ... # SQLite, audio, exports, review, research ├── static/ # Shared desktop/mobile interface ├── assets/ # Bundled renderers and icons ├── desktop/ # Electron and installer build ├── ios-native/ # Experimental native client ├── tests/ # Regression/API tests ├── scripts/smoke_workspace.py # Browser/API/real-media test └── docs/ # Guide, screenshots, verification ``` ## Configuration, data and privacy Settings saves `connections.json` in the active data directory. Keys remain server-side, are omitted from responses and never appear in media URLs. Blank inputs preserve stored keys. Local credentials are plaintext files protected by filesystem permissions, not an encrypted vault. `.env` supplies initial/default `PRIMARY_LLM`, Gemini settings, Ollama host/text/vision/embedding settings and `OLLAMA_NUM_CTX`. Saved routes control new jobs. `OCE_DATA_DIR` overrides storage; `OCE_PORT` controls the standalone entry point. Desktop manages its available port and optional library folder. Storage defaults: `data/` in a source checkout; `%LOCALAPPDATA%/ResearchPal` on installed Windows; `~/Library/Application Support/ResearchPal` on frozen macOS; `~/.researchpal` on other frozen systems. Back up with the app stopped before moving data. Reindex after any embedding-model change, including same-dimension changes. Local-first does not mean offline-only. Cloud models receive source/prompts; OCR servers receive page images; web research contacts external services; Edge needs internet. Ollama uses its configured host. Windows speech and slide assembly run locally; device voice connectivity varies. Documented/desktop backends bind to loopback and reject cross-origin browser requests. There is no multi-user login. Shared/public hosting needs separate authentication/deployment work. Mobile-browser access requires a deliberately reachable backend; the desktop shell remains loopback-only. ## Verification ```powershell .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m unittest discover -s tests -v ``` The isolated Windows browser test uses Playwright and Microsoft Edge. Audio generation/playback tests are skipped by default: ```powershell .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install playwright .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts/smoke_workspace.py ``` It starts a temporary library/backend, imports synthetic Markdown/PDF/DOCX through the browser, checks source/table/math rendering and sanitization, exercises custom provider settings, generates an editable storyboard through an HTTP fixture, and checks a 390px
